_about: Loading-screen tips: paraphrased advice from real players; source kept for attribution.

tips.tip: In Limited, keep most hands that actually function. A mulligan costs more than a slightly clunky seven.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Mulligans Part II: Limited

tips.tip: Ship hands that only work if you draw exactly the right land and spell soon, and slow hands when your deck must be fast.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Mulligans Part II: Limited

tips.tip: Don't lock in as attacker or defender too early. Reassess your role whenever the board or the matchup changes.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Role Assignment

tips.tip: Find the stage of the game where your deck is strongest and steer toward it. The player with the better late game need not race.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Role Assignment

tips.tip: Count cards, not just mana: paying two cards for an effect is a worse deal than getting the same effect for one.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: The Basics of Card Advantage

tips.tip: One good blocker can turn several of the enemy's small attackers into dead cards. That is card advantage too.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: The Basics of Card Advantage

tips.tip: Take a clearly stronger card over an on-color one. When power is close, take the card that fits your colors.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Signals in Booster Draft

tips.tip: Signals are evidence, never proof. One late card means little; a steady stream of one color means a lot.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Signals in Booster Draft

tips.tip: Creatures only earn value when they attack or block. Playing too passively loses just like playing recklessly.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Attacking and Blocking

tips.tip: Don't cast combat tricks into lots of open mana, and don't count on tricks when blocking: the attacker acts last.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Attacking and Blocking

tips.tip: Ending a turn with unused mana is a warning sign. Check your mana curve and the order you play your spells.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Tempo

tips.tip: Save removal for threats that matter: attackers that endanger your life or blockers that shut down your plan.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Threats and Answers

tips.tip: Threats win games, answers buy time. A deck with no answers struggles to come back from behind.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Threats and Answers

tips.tip: Playing around everything can backfire: every extra turn you allow is another draw for your opponent to find an answer.
tips.name: Reid Duke
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Level One: Playing Safe and Playing Scared

tips.tip: Who's the Beatdown? Every game, work out who must attack and who must defend. Playing the wrong role loses games.
tips.name: Mike Flores
tips.title: Magic theory writer
tips.source: Who's the Beatdown? (1999), as discussed in Reid Duke's Level One: Role Assignment

tips.tip: The number one deckbuilding rule: have a powerful, proactive game plan and know exactly what your deck wants to do.
tips.name: Brian Kibler
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: The Number One Rule (StarCityGames, 2013)

tips.tip: Before adding any card or color, ask how it changes your deck's game plan. Every card should serve the plan.
tips.name: Brian Kibler
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: The Number One Rule (StarCityGames, 2013)

tips.tip: Card quality beats card count: three weak cards from one spell are not automatically better than one strong card.
tips.name: Patrick Chapin
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Innovations - The Theory of Everything (StarCityGames, 2010)

tips.tip: Before trading a card for life or tempo, check that what you gain is worth more than what you give up.
tips.name: Patrick Chapin
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Innovations - The Theory of Everything (StarCityGames, 2010)

tips.tip: Tempo is only worth buying if you have something to do with the time you gain.
tips.name: Patrick Chapin
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: Innovations - The Theory of Everything (StarCityGames, 2010)

tips.tip: 'Draft the good cards' - but good means good for your deck: its colors, curve and synergies, not raw power alone.
tips.name: Sam Black
tips.title: Pro Tour Top 4 (Philadelphia 2011)
tips.source: Draft The Good Cards (StarCityGames, 2012)

tips.tip: Count your playables as you draft. The count tells you how many risky, high-upside picks you can still afford.
tips.name: Sam Black
tips.title: Pro Tour Top 4 (Philadelphia 2011)
tips.source: Draft The Good Cards (StarCityGames, 2012)

tips.tip: Draft cards you actually want to play, and keep a clear picture of how your finished deck will win.
tips.name: Sam Black
tips.title: Pro Tour Top 4 (Philadelphia 2011)
tips.source: Draft The Cards You Want To Play (StarCityGames, 2012)

tips.tip: The higher your curve, the more lands you need. Cheap card draw and mana creatures let you shave a land or two.
tips.name: Frank Karsten
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: How Many Lands Do You Need to Consistently Hit Your Land Drops? (ChannelFireball, 2017)

tips.tip: A normal 60-card land count scales to about 41 lands in a 99-card Commander deck; ramp and cheap draw can trim that.
tips.name: Frank Karsten
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: How Many Lands Do You Need to Consistently Hit Your Land Drops? (ChannelFireball, 2017)

tips.tip: On the draw you see an extra card, so slightly fewer lands can work - but cutting too many means more mulligans.
tips.name: Frank Karsten
tips.title: Hall of Fame
tips.source: How Many Lands Do You Need to Consistently Hit Your Land Drops? (ChannelFireball, 2017)

tips.tip: Play enough lands in Commander, around 39-40: long games demand land drops and the mana to recast your commander.
tips.name: Gavin Verhey
tips.title: Wizards of the Coast designer, Good Morning Magic host
tips.source: Good Morning Magic Offers Three Commander Tips (StarCityGames, 2020)

tips.tip: Don't rely only on big bombs. Plenty of cheap spells let you interact early and cast two spells a turn later.
tips.name: Gavin Verhey
tips.title: Wizards of the Coast designer, Good Morning Magic host
tips.source: Good Morning Magic Offers Three Commander Tips (StarCityGames, 2020)

tips.tip: Pack a few answers to artifacts, enchantments and graveyards. In two-player games one such answer can decide it.
tips.name: Gavin Verhey
tips.title: Wizards of the Coast designer, Good Morning Magic host
tips.source: Good Morning Magic Offers Three Commander Tips (StarCityGames, 2020)

tips.tip: Build order: commander first, then synergy cards, then fill gaps in card draw, ramp, removal, sweepers and threats.
tips.name: Gavin Verhey
tips.title: Wizards of the Coast designer, Good Morning Magic host
tips.source: Good Morning Magic Teaches How To Build A Commander Deck (StarCityGames)

tips.tip: Ramp means extra lands early, so your big spells arrive on time. Cultivate-style spells are among the best.
tips.name: Sheldon Menery
tips.title: Commander Rules Committee founding member
tips.source: Commander Fundamentals: Ramp (StarCityGames, 2018)

tips.tip: Fixing a color or fetching a land to hand is not ramp. Only effects that put extra lands into play truly ramp.
tips.name: Sheldon Menery
tips.title: Commander Rules Committee founding member
tips.source: Commander Fundamentals: Ramp (StarCityGames, 2018)
